lines.text: A stock exchange matches orders in an order book. That works because every share is identical, and price is the only question.
Real estate breaks all of that. No two buildings are alike, value is a vector, and buyers and sellers rank each other, differently.
So instead: a two-sided ranked matching market, where standing intents on both sides score each other.
It runs on three objects. The asset enters as an attested vector: income, cap rate, lease term, tenant credit. Each value carries its source, a timestamp and a confidence.
The buy mandate never names an asset. It scores them.
The credit box scores the asset, given who is buying it. And the seller ranks the bids.
Take mandate M, zero four one seven. Hard filters first: logistics, Germany, ten to twenty-five million euros, a cap rate of at least five point two five percent. Fail one, and the asset is out.
Every other dimension maps to a utility, from zero to one. Cap rate climbs from five point two five to seven percent, then caps.
Lot size is a plateau. Tenant credit is stepped: investment grade scores one, double-B point six, single-B point two.
Confidence decays with each attestation's age. So a six point two percent cap rate attested last week outranks six point four from five months ago.
Weights combine it all: cap rate forty-five, lease term twenty-five, credit twenty, vacancy ten. But floors come first. Vacancy over five percent zeroes the score, whatever the yield.
Near-ties go to longer lease term, then lower capex. Never to who arrived first. Each mandate now holds a ranked book.
Lenders don't quote the asset, or the buyer. They quote the pair.
Credit box L one fires at fifty-five percent loan-to-value. L two, at sixty. L three stays silent: the sponsor is below its tier. And no attested income, no quote.
Price depends on debt, and debt on price. So, test one. Net operating income of eight hundred thousand euros. A price of thirteen million.
L one lends the least of three tests: seven point one five million by loan-to-value, nine point four seven by debt service cover, ten point six seven by debt yield. Loan-to-value binds.
That leaves five point eight five million of equity. The engine solves for the highest price that still meets the buyer's twelve percent return, and bids that. Or the ask, if lower.
So a more generous credit box raises the bid, directly.
Sellers score bids beyond price: certainty, speed, conditions. A firm term sheet can beat a higher bid with no debt behind it.
Clearing is deferred acceptance. Each mandate proposes to the top asset in its book.
Each asset tentatively holds the proposal its seller prefers, and releases the rest.
Released mandates move down their books, re-quoting debt for the new pair.
When nobody moves, the set is stable. No asset and mandate would both prefer each other to what they hold. So no one gains by going around the platform.
And it never stops. New attestations, amended mandates, filled credit boxes and rate moves each re-run the affected pairs. Stop attesting, and your asset sinks in every book.
Visibility is set per object, up to double-blind, where neither side sees the other until mutual scores clear a threshold.
The engine is known mathematics. What no one has had is an asset that arrives as an attested vector, and a credit box that can trust it.
Matching is a data outcome.
